blocks.text: Sorting is a fundamental problem in computer science, and understanding elementary sorting algorithms provides a foundation for more advanced techniques.

blocks.markdown: In this lesson, we will explore three elementary sorting algorithms: insertion sort, selection sort, and bubble sort. These algorithms, while not the most efficient for large datasets, are crucial for understanding the basics of algorithm design and analysis.

blocks.title: Insertion Sort
blocks.text: Insertion sort builds the sorted array one element at a time by repeatedly taking the next element and inserting it into the correct position among the previously sorted elements.

blocks.caption: Time complexity of insertion sort in the worst case.

blocks.title: Insertion Sort Example
blocks.prompt: Sort the array [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3] using insertion sort.

steps.text: Start with the first element, 5, which is trivially sorted.

blocks.title: Selection Sort
blocks.text: Selection sort repeatedly selects the smallest (or largest, depending on sorting order) element from the unsorted portion and swaps it with the first unsorted element.

blocks.caption: Time complexity of selection sort in the worst case.

blocks.title: Selection Sort Example
blocks.prompt: Sort the array [29, 10, 14, 37, 13] using selection sort.

steps.text: Select the smallest element in [29, 10, 14, 37, 13] and swap with 29.
Select the smallest element in [29, 14, 37, 13] and swap with 29.
Select the smallest element in [14, 37, 29] and swap with 14.
Select the smallest element in [37, 29] and swap with 37.

blocks.title: Bubble Sort
blocks.text: Bubble sort repeatedly steps through the list, compares adjacent elements, and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. The pass through the list is repeated until the list is sorted.

blocks.caption: Time complexity of bubble sort in the worst case.

blocks.title: When to Use Insertion Sort
blocks.text: Insertion sort is particularly efficient for small datasets or datasets that are already partially sorted, where it can achieve nearly linear performance.

points: Insertion, selection, and bubble sort have quadratic time complexity in the worst case.
Insertion sort is efficient for small or nearly sorted datasets.
All three algorithms have a space complexity of $O(1)$.
